records.claim: Acts is preserved in early papyri and major Greek codices, with P45, P53, P74, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae contributing different portions and textual profiles.

Greek and Latin Psalter traditions number many psalms differently from the Masoretic tradition because they combine Psalms 9-10 and 114-115, divide Psalms 116 and 147, and transmit Psalm 151 beyond the 150-psalm count.

Old Greek Job is substantially shorter than the Masoretic form in much of the poetry and also contains expansions, while Qumran preserves Hebrew fragments and an Aramaic targum. Translation and textual criticism should therefore identify the witness in view rather than treating every ancient form as verbally identical.

The Great Isaiah Scroll is an almost complete sixty-six-chapter witness broadly aligned with the Masoretic tradition but containing thousands of orthographic and substantive differences; other Qumran Isaiah manuscripts and pesharim show active transmission and interpretation.

The chapter 3 speaker turns toward hope by recalling steadfast love, mercies, and faithfulness.
Daniel survives in substantially distinct Old Greek and Theodotionic versions, with especially important differences in chapters 4-6 and in the form and placement of additions.
Old Greek and Theodotionic Daniel must be compared passage by passage; neither label means that every difference has one cause.
Jude addresses called people described as beloved in God and kept for or by Jesus, with textual variation in the wording.
Jude recalls rescue from Egypt followed by destruction of those who did not believe, while the subject in verse 5 has a major textual variant.
A further instruction combines mercy with fear and hatred of a garment stained by flesh.
One well-attested form directs mercy toward people who doubt or dispute.
The letter directs rescue of others by snatching them from fire.
Beloved in God and kept for or by Jesus in verse 1 reflects a textual and grammatical question; theology should not be built as if only one wording and construal existed.
Verses 22-23 have major variants affecting whether two or three groups receive mercy, rescue, or fear. Translation and pastoral policy must not conceal this instability.
Discipline and rescue language call for discerning mercy; they do not authorize coercion, surveillance, spiritual abuse, forced confession, or removal of consent.
Verse 5 reads Jesus, Lord, or God in different witnesses and editions. The Jesus reading makes an unusually explicit christological exodus claim; exact wording requires textual review.

Codex Bezae and related versional witnesses preserve a substantially distinctive text of Acts often called Western, whose individual readings require case-by-case judgment.
Masoretic Haggai, Old Greek Aggaios, Judean Desert copies of the Twelve, and other versions attest transmission and textual plurality in difficult passages.

Masoretic Joel is commonly divided into four chapters, while Old Greek Ioel and many English Bibles use three; the spirit oracle is Joel 3:1-5 MT but Joel 2:28-32 in common English numbering.
Masoretic four-chapter and common English three-chapter numbering must be stated at every affected locator so that Joel 3 and 4 are not confused.
Old Greek Ioel is an ancient translation and textual witness, not merely a Christian edition of Joel.

Luke's Lord's Prayer is shorter than Matthew's in the earliest recoverable text, while manuscripts show harmonizing expansions; its petitions concern God's name, kingdom, daily provision, forgiveness, and testing.

Luke 22:19b-20, including the second cup and new-covenant language, is present in many major witnesses but absent in important Western witnesses; shorter-text, longer-text, and harmonization models remain debated.
Codex Sinaiticus preserves 2 Timothy, while the surviving Codex Vaticanus ends before the Pastoral Epistles and is not a witness to this book.
